source.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
source.authors: M. Magill; F. Qureshi; H. de Haan

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Measures representation similarity across random initializations and task parameters using SVCCA, and validates layer generality with a transfer-learning protocol. These are conceptual tests of convergence/general representations, not the original sources’ method.
record.gate_note: The study measures SVCCA similarity between network layers trained at the same or different source positions, and reports a seed-reproducibility measure and task-specificity measure. Transfer-learning losses are also reported. Results used only to describe implementation or training performance are not recorded as claim rows. Width-sweep plot values are figure-only; individual numeric values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: It trains same-architecture fully connected networks from four random seeds per task. It measures cross-seed SVCCA similarity (reproducibility) per layer and width. This bears directly on V3, using a different method (SVCCA rather than neuron matching) in a new setting (PDE-solving networks).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude the first layer is general, the second somewhat less so, the third general in wide but specific in narrow networks, and the fourth specific up to width 192. SVCCA and transfer learning agree, SVCCA is much faster, and first-layer components act as generalized coordinates. They caution that very wide networks may be under-converged.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SVCCA layer similarity and a transfer-learning validation protocol to study generality in fully connected differential-equation networks; it does not reproduce either original source’s experiments. Compares random seeds and source-position parameters in one architecture and problem family.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with layer and network width. The paper reports that the third layer becomes more general with increasing width in the transfer experiment, while patterns in very wide networks may be affected by under-convergence. At width 16 the layers appear more general than expected and at width 20 more specific than expected. SVCCA component vectors were numerically unstable across repeated analyses, although correlation vectors were stable.

fits_no_version.finding: First and second layers learn similar SVCCA representations across networks trained on different source positions (different objectives). Deeper layers are progressively task-specific, and transfer-learning specificity agrees.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-layer representations converge across related tasks, while deeper-layer convergence depends on the training objective.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (venue stated in metadata); the text labels the paper a preprint and work in progress.
record.problems: Only one architecture family and one parametrized PDE family are studied; four random initializations are used per source position. Error bars for reproducibility and specificity are approximate because correlations among measured values are ignored. The authors note numerical instability in individual SVCCA components and possible under-convergence in very wide networks. Transfer-learning validation covers only selected widths and two source positions.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports transfer-learning results for widths 8, 16, 20, and 24, including losses by number of transferred layers and transfer-specificity comparisons in Figure 4. These are not extracted as separate rows because they evaluate layer transferability rather than the representation-mapping methods named in V4. Figure 3 specificity values for widths other than 20 are also omitted; the width-dependent qualitative trends are noted in method_sensitivity. Figure 3 intrinsic dimensionality results are outside the tested versions.

untested.parts: No comparison across architectures, objectives, data or modalities as models scale.
No vision-language or paired cross-modal data.
Individual-unit correspondence is not tested; only subspace similarity (SVCCA) is measured.
No representation mapping, stitching or relative representations. Transfer of frozen layers is reported only as task-generality.
No test of recurring interpretable features across different models.
No alternative similarity metrics or input distributions compared.
Causes of alignment and plateaus across model families are not tested.

missing.what: Aggregate trend: cross-seed reproducibility rises with width for all layers. It is lower for deeper layers, except the fourth layer at very large widths.

Cross-seed first-layer SVCCA components at width 192 share the same 9-dimensional structure with correlations near 1. Individual components are numerically unstable, so the subspace is shared but not the basis.

record.verdict_notes: V7 was dropped as a tested version: the cross-task rows measure task specificity, not completeness or causes of convergence among independently trained models. Width-specific reproducibility values are figure-only. The y-axis of Fig 3(b) spans 0.80–1.00, so every layer and width shares most of its dimensionality across seeds.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, data or modalities as they scale in size and capability.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language models.

Tests same-architecture networks trained from different random initializations on the same parametrized boundary-value problem. It does not identify individual units or establish that shared components are interpretable features.
The transfer-learning experiment freezes donor layers in recipient networks, but the study does not test a mapping between representations, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired alignment.
Visualizes layer components but does not test whether the same interpretable features or circuits recur across different models.

Does not systematically compare similarity metrics or vary metric settings or input distributions. It compares SVCCA-based generality with transfer-learning generality, not alternative similarity metrics.

Tests incomplete and task-dependent alignment across a family of related problems. It does not test whether shared training data or objectives cause alignment instead of a common model of reality, nor whether alignment plateaus across different model families.
